summary: A 1975 proposal for changes to the protocol between hosts and IMPs, including addressing hosts on more than 63 IMPs and other backward compatible expansions. It was replaced by RFC 704. See also RFC 690 and RFC 692.

plainLanguage.summary: The network was growing past its address limit. This note suggests making room for more machines without breaking old ones.

questions: how did the imp host protocol change in 1975
how many imps could the arpanet address
subtitle: A 1975 sketch of how the IMP/host protocol would grow past 63 IMPs while staying backward compatible.

tldr.problem: The ARPA Network was nearing the limit of the existing IMP/host protocol, with almost 60 IMPs already in service.
tldr.mechanism: The leader grows from two to five 16-bit words, the address field grows to 24 bits, and several new fields are added, with old and new formats supported side by side.
tldr.outcome: This was a design sketch, updated by RFC 690 and replaced by RFC 704.

today: This note was updated by RFC 690 and replaced by RFC 704. It is a historical design sketch from June 1975.

sections.title: Goals of the Expansion
sections.content:
This note by David C. Walden sketches an expansion of the IMP/host and host/IMP protocol. It includes the possibility of addressing hosts on more than 63 IMPs. The intent is to correct existing limits without fundamental changes to the philosophy of the protocol, because BBN could not undertake massive changes on a time scale that fit the short term needs of the network.

Readers are assumed to know Section 3 of BBN Report 1822, and the expanded protocol is described as backwards compatible.
sections.plainLanguage: The network was getting crowded. Instead of rebuilding it, the builders planned small upgrades that would not break what already worked.

sections.title: Changes to the Leader and Fields
sections.content:
The leader grows from two to five 16-bit words. The address field becomes 24 bits: 16 bits of IMP address and 8 bits of host address. A new optional message length field, 13 bits wide, lets the source host tell the IMP subnetwork the message length in bits so buffers can be used better.

The handling type field grows to eight bits, allowing parallel message streams between pairs of hosts, such as priority, non-priority, set packets per message, unordered messages and guaranteed capacity (only some available in the near term). A source host may also choose a fixed number of packets per multi-packet message, such as two or five, so the IMP network need not use eight packet-buffers for reassembly.

Other changes: unordered (type-3) messages are indicated by a handling type, which is a slight backward incompatibility for about three hosts; the For/From IMP bit is dropped and fake host addresses become the four highest host numbers (the IMP Teletype is host 252); and the IMP to host NOP gains a parameter giving the host's IMP and host number.
sections.plainLanguage: The address label gets bigger, with room for a bigger city number and a house number. There is also a new box on the label for how long the letter is.

sections.title: Compatibility and Flow Control
sections.content:
The IMPs will support old and new formats in parallel for the foreseeable future. A host chooses its format through the format of its host to IMP NOP message, and may switch back and forth for debugging. The IMP initializes by sending several NOP messages of each type. A host using the old format cannot address IMPs numbered above 63, but IMPs will convert between formats wherever possible.

The note also promises a non-blocking host interface, so the IMP can refuse a message without blocking the host interface and ask the host to resend later. The maximum message length may be reduced by a few bits. An implementation schedule would follow.
sections.plainLanguage: Old and new labels will both work for a long time. A computer picks the style it likes, and the post office translates between them.
